title: Five Principles for Effective Questioning
author: David Didau
summary: Didau presents a systematic approach to classroom questioning, arguing that it is among the most powerful tools for student learning. He emphasizes that effective questioning is not merely a collection of techniques but an intentional practice grounded in clear purpose. The five principles—starting with purpose, ensuring everyone thinks, expecting participation from all, treating answers as worth shaping, and building sequences of questions that develop thought—provide a framework for transforming questioning from ritual exchange into genuine cognitive engagement. Didau distinguishes between questions designed to check attention, questions that probe understanding, and questions that test mastery, arguing that conflating these purposes undermines effectiveness. The article emphasizes the critical role of wait time and illustrates how diagnostic questioning reveals student misconceptions and supports deeper learning.
points: Effective questioning distinguishes between checking attention, probing understanding, and testing mastery—conflating these purposes undermines learning.
Teachers ask hundreds of questions daily, making questioning a primary mechanism for directing attention and checking understanding.
Wait time of 3+ seconds significantly improves the length and quality of student responses.
Process questions that ask 'how' and 'why' are more diagnostic than surface-level questions.
Questioning is the art of making thought public, allowing teachers to detect misconceptions and support learning.
quotes: Before deciding how to ask questions, we need to be clearer about what questions are for . If modelling is the art of making expert performance visible, and scaffolding is the art of making difficulty manageable, then questioning is the art of making thought public. It allows teachers to check attention, secure understanding, develop mastery and prepare students to express ideas with enough precision to support more developed, independent responses. Used badly, questioning becomes a ritual exchange between teacher and student, a way of creating the appearance of engagement.
context: Questioning is the art of making thought public, allowing teachers to detect misconceptions and support learning.
